question_matrix.question: The main research hypothesis
question_matrix.finding: The primary question asks whether generated images assigned higher learned human-preference scores are harder for binary image detectors. The main result is a positive aggregate score–correctness association, especially above each generator’s score-density peak. Sections 3–4 investigate it before Section 5 applies the results to patch selection.
question_matrix.limitations: This is a tendency over selected populations, not a universal image-level rule or a causal law.

question_matrix.question: Formal definitions of perceived image quality
question_matrix.finding: Quality is operationalized through pretrained image-and-text human-preference predictors, rather than a new psychophysical definition. The authors distinguish individual-image assessment from FID/IS distribution measures. Such scores may mix visual appeal and prompt alignment; neither is identical to photorealism, absence of forensic artifacts or human authenticity accuracy.
question_matrix.limitations: No new direct human-quality rating panel, human authenticity experiment or separately calibrated photorealism measurement is reported.

question_matrix.question: Human-preference predictors and their versions
question_matrix.finding: Main analyses use ImageReward (Xu2023) and Human Preference Score v2 (Wu2023a); Appendix B1 adds MPS (Zhang2024b). Images and original generation prompts normally form the scoring inputs. Appendix B2 replaces the score-input prompt with the generated image’s BLIP-2 caption, while clustering uses empty text in ImageReward.
question_matrix.limitations: The paper names families/publication versions but does not pin exact checkpoint revisions, hashes, several preprocessing settings or MPS dimension selection. No model weights were obtained.

question_matrix.question: Exact text-to-image generator families
question_matrix.finding: The main four models are Stable Diffusion2.1, SDXL1.0, Stable Diffusion3 and PixArt-alpha. Appendices A1/B1 add FLUX.1[dev] and Infinity, covering diffusion/transformer and autoregressive generation. Auxiliary user-created closed-source samples are Midjourneyv6 and DALLE3; they are not another controlled generation of the same4000 prompts.
question_matrix.limitations: Exact checkpoint commits, inference steps, guidance values, seeds and negative/modifier strings are not printed. HF metadata declares some fields but their actual row values were not inspected.

question_matrix.question: Prompt sources and prompt-length distribution
question_matrix.finding: COCO, CC3M, LAION-Aesthetic and SA-1B supply original image content. Captions come from BLIP-2, InternVL2-8B with varied instructions, existing COCO captions and existing SA-1B captions. Filtering and length balancing produce4000 captions, spanning under10 to over120 words. The paper groups short prompts<=20, medium21–40 and long>40 words.
question_matrix.limitations: Per-bin counts, source proportions, exact filtering rules and captioner instructions are unspecified. Medium prompts can score above the shortest prompts; the result is not simply shorter-is-always-better.

question_matrix.question: Source-image and prompt-content dependencies
question_matrix.finding: Each of4000 prompts is used once for each of six generators, implying24000 synthetic images; the author-linked HF card independently declares24000 fake rows, without verifying their contents. Corresponding real images join clustering but are omitted from subsequent fake-image analyses. The manuscript says generated images match paired-real compression format/quality.
question_matrix.limitations: 4000 captions do not establish4000 UNIQUE source photographs or statistically independent prompts. Source reuse, multiple caption variants, prompt groups and their dependencies are not exhaustively identified or deduplicated.

question_matrix.question: Detector identities and training provenance
question_matrix.finding: The six principal detector variants are NPR, RINE, CoDE, SuSy, DRCT(Conv-B) and DRCT(CLIP), run with official pretrained weights/configurations and commonly center-cropped without resizing. Section5 additionally evaluates SSP, retrained on the GenImage all-generator mixture with claimed real/fake compression alignment after poor transfer from official single-generator checkpoints. Main averages contain five end-to-end variants and NPR; patch tests contain seven variants, including two fingerprint methods.
question_matrix.limitations: Exact weight hashes, all original training-image identities and training overlap are not enumerated. No checkpoints/training data were retrieved. An averaged score trend is not proof of the same relation for every individual detector.

question_matrix.question: Image-quality score distributions
question_matrix.finding: Figures1/6/8 show per-generator preference-score histograms and average correctness curves. Figures2/7/9 reverse grouping by the0–6 detectors making correct predictions on each generated image. Section3.2 uses30 equal-width score-range segments. Distributions and trends differ by generator and preference model; several low-score ranges and MPS curves are visibly nonmonotonic.
question_matrix.limitations: Exact bin counts, point data and uncertainty are not tabulated. No precise values are inferred from unlabelled curve coordinates, and sparse tails cannot establish universal monotonicity.

question_matrix.question: Detection metrics and class-prior conditions
question_matrix.finding: Main correctness and Table2 concern synthetic images only: one image’s average is the number of six binary correct predictions divided by6. It is a class-conditional correctness/recall quantity at the frozen detector thresholds, not detector confidence or balanced all-image accuracy. Table3 separately lists all-image ACC, AP, ACC_fake and ACC_real.
question_matrix.limitations: Class-prior pooling, exact sample denominators, decision thresholds and AP implementation details are incompletely specified. Do not assume deployment priors or balanced accuracy. Appendix B4 does not clearly specify the population/weighting behind Table5.

question_matrix.question: Within-generator versus across-generator correlations
question_matrix.finding: The main curves condition on generator. Figure4 uses retained-cluster means within each main generator: Pearson r0.3698–0.6108, with printed p0.00003–0.02049. Section4.3 pools cluster averages from four generators and includes generator-indicator intercepts to account for different baseline accuracies.
question_matrix.limitations: Grouped, feature-selected cluster correlations differ from unbiased individual-image correlations. Intercept adjustment does not control all generator interactions or residual content/source confounding.

question_matrix.question: Quality-score versus correctness relationships
question_matrix.finding: The main endpoint is observed binary correctness, including the integer count0–6, rather than confidence probabilities or margins. Higher-score groups tend to be easier above distribution peaks, but distorted-character and porthole clusters can have low scores and high detectability. Patch AP and real/fake tradeoffs are separate endpoints.
question_matrix.limitations: No claim of monotonicity for every interval, every image or every detector is justified. Confidence, classification correctness and preference score remain different variables.

question_matrix.question: Generator-level confounding
question_matrix.finding: Generator-specific baseline difficulty is explicitly acknowledged and mitigated with separate intercepts in cluster-level regression. Per-generator plots reduce simple between-generator confounding, while extra model families widen descriptive coverage.
question_matrix.limitations: Training data, architecture, resolution, inference settings, modifiers and preference-model biases may still covary. The adjustment does not identify a causal quality effect or guarantee slope transfer to future generators.

question_matrix.question: Content and prompt confounding
question_matrix.finding: Prompt length co-varies with scene/entity complexity and color descriptions. Table4 shows color terms in14.2/37.9/63.2% of0–9/10–19/20–29-word prompts and saturation0.47 with versus0.40 without color terms over prompts under30 words. Generated-image BLIP-2 captions replace original score-input prompts to probe text-alignment effects.
question_matrix.limitations: Caption source, scene content, modifier choices and image provenance are not fully randomized or source-group controlled. Caption substitution reduces one proxy issue; it is not human validation or complete confound removal.

question_matrix.question: Saturation, contrast, texture and complexity analyses
question_matrix.finding: AppendixA3 measures lightness by mean HSV value, contrast by pixel-intensity RMS/standard deviation, saturation by mean HSV saturation, sharpness by grayscale Laplacian variance, texture by Canny-edge-pixel density, and structural complexity by square root of SAM2 segment count. Low-level coefficients have matching positive lightness/contrast/saturation/texture and negative sharpness/complexity signs across accuracy and preference targets.
question_matrix.limitations: These are operational proxies. SAM2 segmentation settings, edge thresholds and several exact implementations are unreported; complexity, semantic content and texture are not independently randomized properties.

question_matrix.question: Clustering and regression procedures
question_matrix.finding: K-means k50 uses ImageReward features of center224x224 patches and empty text. Real images take part in clustering and are excluded from subsequent fake analysis. Clusters with fewer than30 generated images are dropped. Standardized least-squares regression fits cluster means pooled across four generators, with source-indicator intercepts. DINOv2 features reduced by PCA to6 dimensions provide a high-level comparison.
question_matrix.limitations: Retained cluster totals, seeds/repeats, exact checkpoints, PCA fitting partition, held-out regression validation and coefficient uncertainty are not specified. Fit R-squared is not held-out detection accuracy.

question_matrix.question: Statistical robustness and confidence intervals
question_matrix.finding: Figure4 reports eight r/p pairs. Low-level regression R-squared is0.77 for accuracy,0.81 for ImageReward and0.74 for HPSv2; the six-PC counterparts are0.76,0.76,0.68. Additional generators, another proxy and caption substitution test descriptive robustness.
question_matrix.limitations: No confidence intervals, bootstrap/repeated-seed uncertainty, coefficient significance tests, multiplicity correction or prompt/source-group dependence adjustment is reported. Table5 underlining denotes a magnitude threshold over10%, not inferential significance.

question_matrix.question: Data-selection and evaluation leakage safeguards
question_matrix.finding: Documented safeguards include frozen official detectors, paired-real compression matching and external patch evaluation beyond the four regression-analysis generators. AppendixA6 excludes SD2.1/SDXL already used for analysis, commonly trained/similar generators such as SD1.4/1.5, and images<=256x256 with little patch-selection room.
question_matrix.limitations: The design selects detectors that already generalize and eligible image sizes. No full deduplication against detector/preference-model training sets is documented. SSP trains on the GenImage generator mixture while evaluation includes GenImage Midjourney; exact within-dataset splitting is not specified sufficiently to prove absence of leakage.

question_matrix.question: Generalization across detector families
question_matrix.finding: Aggregate observations involve six detector variants and extend to eight generated-image sources. Individual patch outcomes differ: RINE AP90.2→91.9 but ACC75.0→74.2; DRCTCLIP Easiest AP88.4→86.7; NPR Hardest AP78.6 versusEasiest74.6; SSP Hardest AP81.0 versusEasiest77.4. Interventions also differ by family.
question_matrix.limitations: This supports conditional family-specific responses, not one universal easy patch, a guaranteed all-detector quality relation, or gains in every metric.

question_matrix.question: Dependence on quality-score proxies versus direct human judgments
question_matrix.finding: Preference scores come from pretrained predictors rather than new human ratings of the24000 generated images. The third preference model and BLIP-2 caption substitution probe proxy robustness but do not turn predicted preferences into observed human judgments.
question_matrix.limitations: Prior human alignment of a predictor does not establish current-image subjective quality, photorealism or human susceptibility. No new human authenticity experiment is reported.

question_matrix.question: Correlational versus causal interpretation
question_matrix.finding: The principal finding is correlational. The paper discusses potential feature confounders, then shows inconsistent responses to lightness/contrast/saturation/sharpness interventions. Half-contrast changes RINE31.8→15.7 but NPR66.8→89.1. Low-score character/porthole outliers and inconsistent real-image trends further limit a universal account.
question_matrix.limitations: Transformations can alter several properties. Regression, clustering and selective patch improvements do not establish a uniform causal effect of image quality or any one visual characteristic.

current_authoritative_paper.authors: Yao Xiao; Weiyan Chen; jiahao chen; Zijie Cao; Weijian Deng; Binbin Yang; Ziyi Dong; Xiangyang Ji; Wei Ke; Pengxu Wei; Liang Lin
current_authoritative_paper.abstract: Current AI-Generated Image (AIGI) detection approaches predominantly rely on binary classification to distinguish real from synthetic images, often lacking interpretable or convincing evidence to substantiate their decisions. This limitation stems from existing AIGI detection benchmarks, which, despite featuring a broad collection of synthetic images, remain restricted in their coverage of artifact diversity and lack detailed, localized annotations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a fine-grained benchmark towards eXplainable AI-Generated image Detection, named X-AIGD, which provides pixel-level, categorized annotations of perceptual artifacts, spanning low-level distortions, high-level semantics, and cognitive-level counterfactuals. These comprehensive annotations facilitate fine-grained interpretability evaluation and deeper insight into model decision-making processes. Our extensive investigation using X-AIGD provides several key insights: (1) Existing AIGI detectors demonstrate negligible reliance on perceptual artifacts, even at the most basic distortion level. (2) While AIGI detectors can be trained to identify specific artifacts, they still substantially base their judgment on uninterpretable features. (3) Explicitly aligning model attention with artifact regions can increase the interpretability and generalization of detectors. The data and code are available at: https://github.com/Coxy7/X-AIGD.

current_canonical_bibliography.title: Unveiling Perceptual Artifacts: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Interpretable AI-Generated Image Detection
current_canonical_bibliography.authors: Yao Xiao; Weiyan Chen; jiahao chen; Zijie Cao; Weijian Deng; Binbin Yang; Ziyi Dong; Xiangyang Ji; Wei Ke; Pengxu Wei; Liang Lin
current_canonical_bibliography.abstract: Current AI-Generated Image (AIGI) detection approaches predominantly rely on binary classification to distinguish real from synthetic images, often lacking interpretable or convincing evidence to substantiate their decisions. This limitation stems from existing AIGI detection benchmarks, which, despite featuring a broad collection of synthetic images, remain restricted in their coverage of artifact diversity and lack detailed, localized annotations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a fine-grained benchmark towards eXplainable AI-Generated image Detection, named X-AIGD, which provides pixel-level, categorized annotations of perceptual artifacts, spanning low-level distortions, high-level semantics, and cognitive-level counterfactuals. These comprehensive annotations facilitate fine-grained interpretability evaluation and deeper insight into model decision-making processes. Our extensive investigation using X-AIGD provides several key insights: (1) Existing AIGI detectors demonstrate negligible reliance on perceptual artifacts, even at the most basic distortion level. (2) While AIGI detectors can be trained to identify specific artifacts, they still substantially base their judgment on uninterpretable features. (3) Explicitly aligning model attention with artifact regions can increase the interpretability and generalization of detectors. The data and code are available at: https://github.com/Coxy7/X-AIGD.

action.task_definition: Section 3.3 defines Authenticity Judgment as real/fake image classification and Perceptual Artifact Detection as prediction of artifact instance regions and one of seven categories. curated:64635535d7b7b6a12a32.title: Unveiling Perceptual Artifacts: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Interpretable AI-Generated Image Detection
curated:64635535d7b7b6a12a32.authors: Yao Xiao; Weiyan Chen; jiahao chen; Zijie Cao; Weijian Deng; Binbin Yang; Ziyi Dong; Xiangyang Ji; Wei Ke; Pengxu Wei; Liang Lin
curated:64635535d7b7b6a12a32.abstract: Current AI-Generated Image (AIGI) detection approaches predominantly rely on binary classification to distinguish real from synthetic images, often lacking interpretable or convincing evidence to substantiate their decisions. This limitation stems from existing AIGI detection benchmarks, which, despite featuring a broad collection of synthetic images, remain restricted in their coverage of artifact diversity and lack detailed, localized annotations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a fine-grained benchmark towards eXplainable AI-Generated image Detection, named X-AIGD, which provides pixel-level, categorized annotations of perceptual artifacts, spanning low-level distortions, high-level semantics, and cognitive-level counterfactuals. These comprehensive annotations facilitate fine-grained interpretability evaluation and deeper insight into model decision-making processes. Our extensive investigation using X-AIGD provides several key insights: (1) Existing AIGI detectors demonstrate negligible reliance on perceptual artifacts, even at the most basic distortion level. (2) While AIGI detectors can be trained to identify specific artifacts, they still substantially base their judgment on uninterpretable features. (3) Explicitly aligning model attention with artifact regions can increase the interpretability and generalization of detectors. The data and code are available at: https://github.com/Coxy7/X-AIGD.

curated:7693a9c0107feaf90e10.title: Are High-Quality AI-Generated Images More Difficult for Models to Detect?
curated:7693a9c0107feaf90e10.authors: Yao Xiao, Yao_Xiao, Binbin Yang, Weiyan Chen, Jiahao Chen, Zijie Cao, ZiYi Dong, Xiangyang Ji, Liang Lin, Wei Ke, Pengxu Wei
curated:7693a9c0107feaf90e10.abstract: The remarkable evolution of generative models has enabled the generation of high-quality, visually attractive images, often perceptually indistinguishable from real photographs to human eyes. This has spurred significant attention on AI-generated image (AIGI) detection. Intuitively, higher image quality should increase detection difficulty. However, our systematic study on cutting-edge text-to-image generators reveals a counterintuitive finding: AIGIs with higher quality scores, as assessed by human preference models, tend to be more easily detected by existing models. To investigate this, we examine how the text prompts for generation and image characteristics influence both quality scores and detector accuracy. We observe that images from short prompts tend to achieve higher preference scores while being easier to detect. Furthermore, through clustering and regression analyses, we verify that image characteristics like saturation, contrast, and texture richness collectively impact both image quality and detector accuracy. Finally, we demonstrate that the performance of off-the-shelf detectors can be enhanced across diverse generators and datasets by selecting input patches based on the predicted scores of our regression models, thus substantiating the broader applicability of our findings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Coxy7/AIGI-Detection-Quality-Paradox.

curated:64635535d7b7b6a12a32.title: Unveiling Perceptual Artifacts: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Interpretable AI-Generated Image Detection
curated:64635535d7b7b6a12a32.authors: Yao Xiao; Weiyan Chen; jiahao chen; Zijie Cao; Weijian Deng; Binbin Yang; Ziyi Dong; Xiangyang Ji; Wei Ke; Pengxu Wei; Liang Lin
curated:64635535d7b7b6a12a32.abstract: Current AI-Generated Image (AIGI) detection approaches predominantly rely on binary classification to distinguish real from synthetic images, often lacking interpretable or convincing evidence to substantiate their decisions. This limitation stems from existing AIGI detection benchmarks, which, despite featuring a broad collection of synthetic images, remain restricted in their coverage of artifact diversity and lack detailed, localized annotations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a fine-grained benchmark towards eXplainable AI-Generated image Detection, named X-AIGD, which provides pixel-level, categorized annotations of perceptual artifacts, spanning low-level distortions, high-level semantics, and cognitive-level counterfactuals. These comprehensive annotations facilitate fine-grained interpretability evaluation and deeper insight into model decision-making processes. Our extensive investigation using X-AIGD provides several key insights: (1) Existing AIGI detectors demonstrate negligible reliance on perceptual artifacts, even at the most basic distortion level. (2) While AIGI detectors can be trained to identify specific artifacts, they still substantially base their judgment on uninterpretable features. (3) Explicitly aligning model attention with artifact regions can increase the interpretability and generalization of detectors. The data and code are available at: https://github.com/Coxy7/X-AIGD.

curated:7693a9c0107feaf90e10.title: Are High-Quality AI-Generated Images More Difficult for Models to Detect?
curated:7693a9c0107feaf90e10.authors: Yao Xiao, Yao_Xiao, Binbin Yang, Weiyan Chen, Jiahao Chen, Zijie Cao, ZiYi Dong, Xiangyang Ji, Liang Lin, Wei Ke, Pengxu Wei
curated:7693a9c0107feaf90e10.abstract: The remarkable evolution of generative models has enabled the generation of high-quality, visually attractive images, often perceptually indistinguishable from real photographs to human eyes. This has spurred significant attention on AI-generated image (AIGI) detection. Intuitively, higher image quality should increase detection difficulty. However, our systematic study on cutting-edge text-to-image generators reveals a counterintuitive finding: AIGIs with higher quality scores, as assessed by human preference models, tend to be more easily detected by existing models. To investigate this, we examine how the text prompts for generation and image characteristics influence both quality scores and detector accuracy. We observe that images from short prompts tend to achieve higher preference scores while being easier to detect. Furthermore, through clustering and regression analyses, we verify that image characteristics like saturation, contrast, and texture richness collectively impact both image quality and detector accuracy. Finally, we demonstrate that the performance of off-the-shelf detectors can be enhanced across diverse generators and datasets by selecting input patches based on the predicted scores of our regression models, thus substantiating the broader applicability of our findings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Coxy7/AIGI-Detection-Quality-Paradox.
